WHAT DOES THIS MEASURE?

Brightness over time, at the same screen location.

1. Relative luminance · Y

A dimensionless value from 0 (black) to 1 (white), calculated from captured sRGB pixels. It is not screen brightness in nits and is not a contrast ratio.

Y = 0.2126R + 0.7152G + 0.0722B

R, G and B are linearized channel values. For an 8-bit channel c, let s=c/255: linear=s/12.92 when s≤0.04045, otherwise ((s+0.055)/1.055)^2.

2. Changes and complete pairs

A general-flash candidate requires two opposing luminance changes, each at least 0.10, with a darker state below 0.80. A black → white → black sequence is one complete pair. The detector counts pairs within a rolling second at each sampled pixel.

The peak is the largest count at any one sampled pixel. Four or more flags review; the flash area may still be below the allowed threshold.

3. Color, timing and evidence

Red candidates use linear-R/(R+G+B) ≥ 0.8 and a CIE 1976 u′v′ change > 0.2 between adjacent captured frames. This heuristic can miss gradual red changes.

The output includes a selected-point Y trace, RGB values, frame min/mean/max Y, observed frame rate, capture gaps and static screenshots. Neither frame averages nor capture-wide ΔY establish a flash.

CONTROLLED EXAMPLES

Compare passing and failing sequences

Analyze generated frames without playing any animation, or open a separate live test page. All live examples require an explicit start. Expected failures assume the flashing field exceeds the WCAG area threshold.

Warning before failing examples: Live failing examples intentionally flash and may trigger seizures, migraines, dizziness or nausea. Do not run them if you or anyone nearby may be sensitive. Synthetic analysis displays numbers only; screenshots remain collapsed and static.

03 / INTERPRETATION

Evidence for a review.
Never an automatic “pass.”

WCAG allows no more than three general or red flashes in any one-second period, or flashes below its area threshold. A flash is a pair of opposing transitions; a single brightness change is not a complete flash.

This prototype tracks luminance excursions at reduced-resolution pixels and uses a separate red-transition heuristic. It flags pixels with more than three completed pairs in a rolling second. It does not combine concurrent flash areas or evaluate a 10-degree visual field.

Test autoplay, video, animations, interaction states, and different viewport sizes. Preserve the test conditions. Review suspicious segments with an established flash-analysis tool before writing a conformance finding.

What can this screening miss?

Small regions, gradual red changes, fine patterns, moving flashes, differently phased regions, offscreen content, short events between captured frames, and protected video. Scrolling and camera motion can also produce false positives. Even a high observed frame rate does not rule out aliasing.
